newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. envoy to bring Clinton message to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy to bring Clinton message to Zaire.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson was expected in Zaire on Monday for talks with the main protagonists in the country's seven-month-old civil war, President Mobutu Sese Seko's son and adviser said on Monday.

Nzanga Mobutu said Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, was carrying a personal message from President Bill Clinton to Mobutu, which he would deliver to the Zairean leader at his camp Tshatshi residence on Tuesday morning.
"He is carrying a personal letter from President Clinton. We don't know yet what it contains," Nzanga told Reuters.
He added that the envoy's visit was part of efforts to bring Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila to the negotiating table to avert civil war reaching Zaire's teeming capital.
The two old foes have both agreed to meet but a neutral venue is one problem. Kabila's insistence that the only item on the agenda is Mobutu's departure is another.
Both the White House and the State Department have been calling for Mobutu, who has ruled the vast Central African country for 32 years, to give way to a transitional government.
Mobutu's MPR party accuses Washington of sponsoring Tutsi-led rebels who control more than half the country.
Richardson is due to fly on from Kinshasa for meetings with Kabila, expected to be in rebel-held territory.
Nzanga said his father had accepted an invitation from President Omar Bongo to meet his arch-foe in Gabon.
"President Mobutu has accepted to go to Gabon. It is closer and easier and its a solution accepted by everybody except Kabila," he said, adding that Kabila was under pressure to change his mind.

Kabila insists that Mobutu come either to Zambia or South Africa. Mobutu, who is convalescing after prostate cancer surgery in August, wants a venue closer to home, and had previously offered the Congolese capital Brazzaville across the river from Kinshasa.
Zaire has accused Zambia of aiding the rebels and looked unlikely to consider the country as a neutral venue.
"Our troops that were in Lubumbashi were attacked from Zambia. Zambia is definitely not a neutral place," one government official said.

International efforts to stage direct talks between the two foes have intensified as rebels step up their advance on Kinshasa. Rebel leaders say they expect the capital to fall within days. Government army commanders say they will fight to the death to defend the city.
